definition: Corroborate means to strengthen a claim or account with independent evidence — a second source that tells the same story.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word corroborate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know corroborate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Flight-recorder data corroborated the pilot's account of a sudden downdraft over the ridge.
Suggest is weaker than corroborate: evidence that merely suggests something leans a claim's way, while corroborating evidence arrives from an independent source and squarely backs it.
Prove goes further than corroborate — corroborating testimony strengthens an account that could still be wrong, but proof is meant to close the question for good.

To verify something is to check its truth yourself — against the records, the math, the original. Corroborate works from outside: you don't re-check the claim, you add a second, independent piece of evidence that tells the same story.

To bolster is to prop something up — any support will do, from money to morale. Corroborate is one specific way of bolstering a claim: an independent source that agrees. Every corroboration bolsters; very little bolstering corroborates.

Corroborate means to strengthen a claim or account with independent evidence — a second source that tells the same story.

A lone seismograph in a Nevada schoolhouse recorded a strange double tremor, and for a week its keepers were accused of an instrument glitch — until stations in Utah and Idaho released their tapes and corroborated the reading, each showing the same two pulses at the same instant.

Corroborate fits because the Utah and Idaho tapes are independent sources agreeing with the first: nobody repaired the Nevada machine or argued on its behalf — separate witnesses told the same story, and that is the word's whole job.
Verify would mean re-checking the Nevada tape itself; prove would claim the question was closed.
And unlike this unit's substantiate, which says how solid the backing is, corroborate points at where it comes from — another voice.
Corroborate lives where claims are contested — courtrooms, labs, newsrooms — and it always implies a second, independent voice.

Keep it apart from two of its neighbors in this unit: substantiate says the backing is solid, and validate says a check was passed, but corroborate says that someone else, separately, tells the same story.
The everyday alternative is back up.

For decades the town's favorite story was pure hearsay: that the 1911 regatta had been cancelled when a freak June snowstorm buried the harbor.
Historians rolled their eyes.
One diary mentioned the storm, but the diarist was eleven years old at the time and writing forty years later.

Then the historical society digitized the lighthouse keeper's daily log, and there it was, in fading ink: 'June 14 -- snow to the knees, no boats out.' A keeper's log could not corroborate every detail of the legend -- nothing in it mentioned the regatta itself -- but on the storm, an independent record now told the same story as the diary.
The society's newsletter put it carefully: one witness makes a tale; two, writing decades apart and never having met, start to make a fact.
